idiom_name: time.Ticker wake-up cadence with time.Since deltas and a fixed-step accumulator
implementation_notes: Go's standard library supplies timing, not a loop: time.NewTicker returns a Ticker holding 'a channel that will send the current time on the channel after each tick', and the documentation warns that 'the ticker will adjust the time interval or drop ticks to make up for slow receivers' - so counting ticks is not counting simulation steps. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - the driver loop is hand-written. Measure elapsed time with time.Now() and time.Since, which use the monotonic reading carried by time.Time, feed a lag accumulator, and use the ticker or a timer purely as a wake-up cadence; give the loop a quit channel instead of a shared boolean so shutdown is race-free (and remember NewTicker panics if the duration is not positive). Since Go 1.23 unreferenced tickers are recoverable by the garbage collector, but calling Stop remains good hygiene for long-lived loops. A worker goroutine may own heavy per-step work, but the loop owns world state.
code_sketch:
const dt = time.Second / 60
prev := time.Now()
var lag time.Duration
ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Second / 120) // wake-up cadence, not a step count
defer ticker.Stop()
for range ticker.C {
    now := time.Now()
    lag += now.Sub(prev)                       // monotonic reading; ticks may drop
    prev = now
    if lag > 250*time.Millisecond { lag = 250 * time.Millisecond }  // clamp
    for lag >= dt { world.Step(dt); lag -= dt }
    render(float64(lag) / float64(dt))         // interpolate
}
pitfalls: time.Ticker drops or stretches ticks for a slow receiver, so never advance the world once per tick; accumulate measured time instead, and note that NewTicker panics on a non-positive duration.
Use the monotonic reading carried by time.Time (Now, Sub, Since) for intervals; UnixNano or time.Unix differences come from the wall clock and jump when it is adjusted.
time.Sleep and ticker granularity are platform-dependent and at-least: sleeping without re-measuring makes the simulation drift, while spinning without any wait burns a core.
A world shared between input goroutines, a renderer and the step loop needs an ownership rule (the loop owns state; channels or a mutex carry deltas) - the race detector is the tool that proves it.
